entities.summary:
The Battle of Thermopylae was a pivotal event in the Persian Wars, fought between the Persian Empire and a coalition of Greek city-states in 480 BCE. Led by King Leonidas of Sparta, a small force of approximately 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians, and 400 Thebans defended a narrow pass against the massive Persian army of over 100,000 soldiers. The bravery and sacrifice of the Greek warriors, despite being vastly outnumbered, galvanized the Greek resistance and paved the way for the eventual defeat of the Persians at the Battle of Plataea in 479 BCE.

The Battle of Thermopylae was a significant turning point in the Persian Wars, showcasing the determination and courage of the Greek people. The battle took place in the narrow pass of Thermopylae, where the Greeks had chosen to fight, and was marked by intense fighting and heavy casualties on both sides. Although the Greeks ultimately lost the battle, their sacrifice and heroism inspired the rest of Greece to rally against the Persians.

The legacy of the Battle of Thermopylae extends far beyond the battlefield. It has become an enduring symbol of Greek courage and resistance, inspiring countless works of art and literature over the centuries. The battle also had a profound impact on the development of Western civilization, influencing the way future generations thought about courage, honor, and sacrifice.

As the Athenian historian Herodotus so eloquently put it, 'The battle of Thermopylae was a contest, not merely of men, but of the very fate of Greece itself.'

This phrase encapsulates the significance of the Battle of Thermopylae, which was a defining moment in the ancient world, shaping the course of Western history and continuing to inspire and captivate people to this day.
